{{Short description|Kepler–Poinsot polyhedron}}
{{Reg polyhedra db|Reg star polyhedron stat table|gsD}}
[[File:Great stellated dodecahedron.stl|thumb|3D model of a great stellated dodecahedron]]
In [[geometry]], the '''great stellated dodecahedron''' is a [[Kepler–Poinsot polyhedron]], with [[Schläfli symbol]] {{math|{{mset|{{frac|5|2}}, 3}}}}. It is one of four [[nonconvex]] [[List of regular polytopes#Non-convex 2|regular polyhedra]].

It is composed of 12 intersecting [[pentagram]]mic faces, with three pentagrams meeting at each vertex.

It shares its [[vertex arrangement]], although not its [[vertex figure]] or [[vertex configuration]], with the [[regular dodecahedron]], as well as being a [[stellation]] of a (smaller) dodecahedron. It is the only dodecahedral stellation with this property, apart from the dodecahedron itself. Its dual, the [[great icosahedron]], is related in a similar fashion to the [[icosahedron]].

It can be constructed by augmenting each face of a regular [[icosahedron]] with a right [[Tetrahedron|triangular pyramid]] of height <math>\sqrt{\frac{7+3\sqrt5}{6}}</math>  times the icosahedron's edge length.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Weisstein |first=Eric W. |title=Great Stellated Dodecahedron |url=https://mathworld.wolfram.com/GreatStellatedDodecahedron.html |access-date=2026-04-09 |website=mathworld.wolfram.com |language=en}}</ref>

If the pentagrammic faces are broken into triangles, it is topologically related to the [[triakis icosahedron]], with the same face connectivity, but much taller [[isosceles]] triangle faces. If the triangles are instead made to invert themselves and excavate the central icosahedron, the result is a [[great dodecahedron]].

The great stellated dodecahedron can be constructed analogously to the pentagram, its two-dimensional analogue, by attempting to stellate the {{mvar|n}}-dimensional [[pentagonal polytope]] (which has pentagonal polytope faces and simplex vertex figures) until it can no longer be stellated; that is, it is its final stellation.

== Formulas ==

For a great stellated dodecahedron with edge length {{mvar|E}} (where {{mvar|E}} represents the length of any edge of the internal icosahedron),

{|  style="height: 300px" align=center
| align="right" | [[Inradius]]: || <math>\quad E \times \frac{\sqrt{5}-1}{2}</math>
|-
| align="right" | [[Midradius]]: || <math>\quad E \times \frac{1+\sqrt{5}}{4}</math>
|-
| align="right" | [[Circumradius]]: || <math>\quad E \times \frac{\sqrt{3}(3+\sqrt{5})}{4}</math>
|-
| align="right" | [[Surface area]]: || <math>\quad E^2 \times 15\sqrt{5+2\sqrt{5}}</math>
|-
| align="right" | [[Volume]]: || <math>\quad E^3 \times \frac{5(3+\sqrt{5})}{4}</math>
|}

==Related polyhedra==
[[File:Great stellated dodecahedron truncations.gif|thumb|right|240px|Animated truncation sequence from {{math|{{mset|{{frac|5|2}}, 3}}}} to {{math|{{mset|3, {{frac|5|2}}}}}}]]
A truncation process applied to the great stellated dodecahedron produces a series of uniform polyhedra. Truncating edges down to points produces the [[great icosidodecahedron]] as a rectified great stellated dodecahedron. The process completes as a birectification, reducing the original faces down to points, and producing the [[great icosahedron]].

The [[Truncation (geometry)|truncated]] ''great stellated dodecahedron'' is a degenerate polyhedron, with 20 triangular faces from the truncated vertices, and 12 (hidden) pentagonal faces as truncations of the original pentagram faces, the latter forming a [[great dodecahedron]] inscribed within and sharing the edges of the icosahedron.{{Dodecahedron stellations}}
